answers.question: How does an O3 frontend module declare its configuration schema so implementers can override its settings? Point to the documentation and implementation.

paragraphs.text: An O3 frontend module declares its configurable settings by writing a **config schema** — a plain JavaScript object whose leaves describe each setting's type, default and validation rules — and registering it with the framework in its entry point. Implementers then override those settings by writing JSON, without touching code.

The documentation lives in the O3 docs repo, in `configuration-system.mdx` (the developer-facing guide) and `configure-o3/overview.mdx` (the implementer-facing guide). The implementation lives in `openmrs-esm-core`, in the `@openmrs/esm-config` package.
## What the documentation says

The config system "provides a framework for making frontend modules configurable by implementers without requiring code changes" [1]. It only applies to developers making a module configurable; implementers configuring an instance should read the Configure O3 guide [2].

The main task for a module author is to "create a config schema for your module … what configuration files should look like, including defaults and validations" [3]. Schemas are optional — a pure library module can skip one [4].

Two implementer-facing docs cover the flip side: how per-module configuration is written, shown with the Programs module's `config-schema.ts` [5], and the fact that O3 ships an implicit schema for every module, giving `Display conditions` and `Translation overrides` without the module declaring them [6].
## The schema file

Each module keeps its schema in a `config-schema.ts` inside `src` [7]. Every leaf is an object, never a raw value, and carries `_`-prefixed keywords: `_type`, `_default`, `_description`, `_validators`, `_elements` [8]. The full keyword reference is in the Schema Reference section [9].

A real example is the login app's schema, which validates login modes with `validators.oneOf`, requires an explicit `loginUrl` for custom/oauth2 providers, and supplies defaults like `'${openmrsSpaBase}/login'` [10]. Types come from the `Type` enum — String, Number, Boolean, Array, Object, UUID and several UUID subtypes [11].
## Where the schema is registered

Modules register the schema in `startupApp()`, the once-per-module setup hook [12]. The call is `defineConfigSchema(moduleName, configSchema)` [13]. `startupApp` is exported from `src/index.ts`, the module's entry point [14].
## The implementation

`defineConfigSchema` is defined in the config package [15]. It does three things: validates the schema, merges it with the implicit schema via `mergeDeepReplace`, and stores the result in the config store keyed by module name, also flagging the module as loaded [15].

The implicit schema is the small object holding `Display conditions` and the translation overrides keys [16]. Because it is merged in automatically, a module cannot redefine or conflict with those keys [17].

The schema shape itself is typed by `ConfigSchema`, whose object index signature allows nested schemas or values recursing to any depth, alongside the optional `_type`, `_validators` and `_elements` keys [18]. The `Type` enum and the validator types sit in the same file [19]. All of it is re-exported to modules through the framework's public entry point [20], which is why modules import `defineConfigSchema`, `Type` and `validator` from `@openmrs/esm-framework`.
## How implementers override and consume settings

Values are merged with a fixed precedence: schema defaults, then config files in load order, then temporary config from the Implementer Tools UI [21]. Nested objects merge deeply but arrays are replaced wholesale [22].

Modules then read the merged result either asynchronously with `getConfig(moduleName)` [23] or, in React, with the `useConfig` hook, which infers the module from the `ComponentContext` set by `getSyncLifecycle`/`getAsyncLifecycle` and merges extension-specific config when used inside an extension [24]. An interface can be declared next to the schema and passed as a type argument for typed access [25].

Extensions can additionally declare their own schema with `defineExtensionConfigSchema`; the extension name must match its `name` in `routes.json`, values live under the extension name, and per-slot `configure` overrides win [26].
## The flow

```mermaid
---
title: Config schema to resolved setting
---
flowchart TD
  schema["src/config-schema.ts"] --> reg["startupApp calls defineConfigSchema"]
  reg --> merge["mergeDeepReplace with implicit schema"]
  merge --> store["config system store"]
  impl["Implementer config files"] --> resolver["config resolver"]
  tools["Implementer Tools temporary config"] --> resolver
  store --> resolver
  resolver --> hook["useConfig or getConfig"]
  hook --> component["Module component"]
```

It enables developers to define schemas that specify what configuration options are available, their types, defaults, and validation rules.

**For implementers**: If you're looking to configure an existing O3 instance (changing logos, translations, module settings, etc.), see the [Configure O3](/docs/configure-o3/overview) guide instead. This guide is for **developers** who want to make their modules configurable.

### How to make a frontend module configurable
You should use the OpenMRS Frontend Framework to make modules configurable.
The main task is to create a config schema for your module. The config schema is what tells the framework what configuration files should look like, including defaults and validations.

**Note**: Configuration schemas are optional. If your module doesn't need any configuration options (for example, if it's a library module like the [React Form Engine](https://github.com/openmrs/openmrs-esm-form-engine-lib) that receives all its configuration through props or function parameters), you don't need to define a schema. The configuration system will still work; modules without schemas use the implicit schema for `Display conditions` and `Translation overrides`.

Every module automatically receives an implicit schema that includes two reserved configuration keys:
- **`Display conditions`** - Used by the extension system to control extension visibility (only relevant for extensions)
- **`Translation overrides`** - Used for per-language translation overrides. See [Configure translations](/docs/configure-o3/configure-translations) for details on how implementers use this feature.

This implicit schema is available immediately, even before you call `defineConfigSchema()`. This allows translation overrides to be loaded early, which is important because the translation system requires them before modules can fully initialize. When you define your custom schema, it is automatically merged with the implicit schema, so you don't need to (and should not) define these reserved keys yourself.

Extensions can have their own configuration schemas that are separate from their parent module's configuration. This is useful when an extension needs configuration options that don't apply to the module as a whole.
To define an extension-specific config schema, use `defineExtensionConfigSchema`:

The extension name should match the `name` property of the extension as defined in `routes.json`. When an extension has its own config schema, base values for that schema are provided under the extension name, not under the module name. `useConfig()` within that extension still returns the module's normal configuration plus the extension's configuration. Extension-specific values take precedence when the same top-level key exists in both places.
Extension configuration values are determined by merging multiple sources in this order:
1. **Extension's base configuration** - Values provided under the extension name when the extension has its own schema, or under the extension module name when it uses the module schema
2. **Slot-specific overrides** - Values from the `configure` object in the slot's configuration (highest precedence)

This merging allows administrators to customize an extension's behavior differently for each slot where it appears. For example, the same extension could have different settings when used in a patient header versus a dashboard.

The `configure` key must match the extension ID assigned to the slot. If you attach the same extension multiple times with instance IDs such as `my-extension#left` and `my-extension#right`, configure those full IDs separately.
